title: Branch and Bound (BnB)
wrong: The entry said the search window runs from the payment plus its fee up to that figure plus what a change output would have cost to create.
fixed: The window's upper bound is the payment plus its fee plus the cost of creating and later spending a change output, which is how Bitcoin Core defines cost_of_change for SelectCoinsBnB in src/wallet/coinselection.cpp (created at the transaction's fee rate, spent at the discard fee rate).
credit: the coin selection chapter's research pass (2026-10-20)

title: Dust
wrong: The entry said the default relay floor has been 0.1 sat/vB since Bitcoin Core 30.0.
fixed: Bitcoin Core 29.1 (September 4, 2025) lowered the default minrelaytxfee and incrementalrelayfee to 100 satoshis per kvB, which is 0.1 sat/vB; 30.0 (October 10, 2025) restated the same two defaults in sat/vB. The entry now dates the change to 29.1 and cites both release notes.
credit: the coin selection chapter's research pass (2026-10-20)

title: Dust Attack
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core's avoid_reuse wallet flag skips coins paid to an address you already spent from, as if every way of spending from the wallet applied the filter.
fixed: It now says the flag marks those coins and sendtoaddress skips them, while Core's other send commands and its GUI do not, so coin control and freezing still do the job by hand. Confirmed on a Bitcoin Core 31.1 regtest node on 2026-10-20.
credit: the coin selection chapter's research pass (2026-10-20)

title: Forced Address Reuse
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core 0.19.0.1 closed the gap left by -avoidpartialspends with the avoid_reuse flag, which marks every address the wallet has spent from and skips coins sent there afterwards, as if every send path applied the filter.
fixed: It now says the flag flags such coins as dirty and that sendtoaddress skips them by default while Core's other send commands and its GUI do not. Confirmed on a Bitcoin Core 31.1 regtest node on 2026-10-20.
credit: the coin selection chapter's research pass (2026-10-20)

title: Use It Once: Why Reusing a Bitcoin Address Is Dangerous
wrong: The closing checklist said Core's optional avoid_reuse flag handles the crumbs, which read as if the flag alone kept a dust crumb from ever being spent.
fixed: It now says the flag keeps sendtoaddress from spending the crumbs, in line with the regtest check of 2026-10-20 that found Core's other send commands and its GUI do not apply the filter.
credit: the coin selection chapter's research pass (2026-10-20)

title: Avoid Reuse (Bitcoin Core)
wrong: The entry said that with the flag on, dirty coins (sent to an address the wallet had already spent from) are left out of coin selection, as if every way of spending from the wallet applied the filter.
fixed: It now says the filter is applied by sendtoaddress alone: in Bitcoin Core's wallet code the dirty-coin check runs only when the command building the transaction asks for it, and only sendtoaddress does, so send, sendmany, sendall, fundrawtransaction, walletcreatefundedpsbt and the GUI spend dirty coins with the flag on. Confirmed on a Bitcoin Core 31.1 regtest node on 2026-10-20, where sendtoaddress answered 'Insufficient funds' and the other five commands each spent the dirty coin.
credit: the coin selection chapter's research pass (2026-10-20)

title: Use It Once: Why Reusing a Bitcoin Address Is Dangerous
wrong: The chapter said Bitcoin Core's avoid_reuse wallet flag skips coins sent to an address after it was spent from, which read as if the whole wallet refused to spend them.
fixed: It now says the flag marks those coins as dirty and keeps sendtoaddress from spending them, while Core's other send commands and its GUI do not apply the filter. Confirmed on a Bitcoin Core 31.1 regtest node on 2026-10-20.
credit: the coin selection chapter's research pass (2026-10-20)

title: Use It Once: Why Reusing a Bitcoin Address Is Dangerous
wrong: The 2013 section said one address per payment means one compromised key costs one payment, and that a key that signs once cannot leak through a repeated nonce, which read as if fresh addresses were the whole defense against a broken random number generator.
fixed: It now says fresh addresses shrink the damage without repairing the generator: if a wallet's random numbers were bad, every key it made with them is suspect, which is why the bitcoin.org alert of 11 August 2013 called for new keys from 'a repaired random number generator', not just for new addresses.

title: Vanity Address
wrong: The entry said that in split-key vanity generation 'neither party ever sees the full private key', listed the 1BitcoinEater burn address among 'famous' vanity addresses, recommended a tool called bitcoin-vanity-search that does not exist, put Taproot bc1p prefixes in the bech32 cost table as if a try cost the same, and said a vanity service 'emails you the seed'.
fixed: The requester publishes a public point, the searcher returns an offset, and the requester adds the two to get the full private key, which only the searcher never learns; the entry says so and tells the reader to check the address before funding it. 1BitcoinEater is described as the opposite construction (hand-written text with a computed checksum, no key search, no key) and linked to the burn-address entry, with BitMEX's 3BMEX deposit addresses as the genuine example. The tools are VanitySearch and vanitygen++, with a note that the original vanitygen is Base58-only. Taproot prefixes take the same number of tries but cost more per try, and a service hands over a private key, not a seed.

title: BIP 360 (Pay-to-Merkle-Root)
wrong: The entry said long-exposure quantum attacks 'become impossible' against P2MR outputs, that P2MR 'fixes' the long exposure of Satoshi-era P2PK keys and reused-address keys, and that BIP-360 and BIP-361 'are designed to land together'.
fixed: BIP-360 says a P2MR output becomes vulnerable to long-exposure attacks whenever one of its scripts reveals a public key, so the protection depends on not reusing keys. P2MR is a destination for coins that move to it and does nothing for keys that stay exposed. Neither BIP mentions the other, and BIP-361 lists a post-quantum signature BIP as its requirement, which P2MR is not. The entry now says all three.

title: BIP 361 (Post Quantum Migration)
wrong: The entry put Phase B 'five years after Phase A activates', said P2PK coins such as Satoshi's could only move 'via the rescue protocol' and reasoned from BIP-32 seeds, said stranding them was 'not the BIP's stated goal', and presented a 2027 to early-2030s arrival for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer as the estimate.
fixed: The draft puts Phase A about three years (160,000 blocks) after BIP-361 activates and Phase B two years after that, about five years in all. Its authors say no rescue protocol is believed possible for P2PK and point to a separate Hourglass proposal instead, list abandoned coins staying unspendable as a benefit ('supply discipline'), and cite 2027 to 2030 as an 'as early as' estimate sourced to McKinsey. The entry now says all of this and adds Taproot outputs as the third way a public key ends up on chain.

title: CRQC (Cryptographically-Relevant Quantum Computer)
wrong: The entry said demonstrated logical (error-corrected) qubit counts remain in the single digits across all hardware platforms, and described superconducting and trapped-ion machines as 'gate-based platforms' in contrast to neutral-atom ones.
fixed: Demonstrated logical qubit counts are in the dozens, not single digits: a neutral-atom processor ran circuits with up to 48 logical qubits in December 2023, on small codes with error detection rather than deep error correction. Neutral-atom processors are gate-based too, so the hardware section now groups platforms by the kind of physical qubit they use and cites the Google Willow and Harvard atom-array demonstrations.

title: ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)
wrong: The entry called P2WPKH and P2WSH legacy address types and said new Taproot outputs use Schnorr 'by default'.
fixed: P2WPKH and P2WSH are SegWit v0 output types, not legacy ones; what they share with P2PKH and P2SH is that they are pre-Taproot and still use ECDSA. Taproot outputs use Schnorr only: BIP 341 key path spends verify a BIP 340 signature and BIP 342 redefines OP_CHECKSIG for Schnorr instead of ECDSA, with no ECDSA option.

title: Key Pool
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core keeps its keypool as a derivation window for gap-limit scanning, with addresses beyond 20 unused derivations not scanned.
fixed: The 20-address gap limit is BIP 44's convention for other HD wallets. Bitcoin Core's keypool is its own lookahead window, raised from 100 to 1,000 keys in 0.15.0 (2017) so a restored backup still finds payments to addresses handed out after it was made.

title: ML-DSA / Dilithium (FIPS 204)
wrong: The entry gave ML-DSA-65 signatures as about 3,293 bytes and ML-DSA-87 signatures as about 4,595 bytes, the sizes in the draft standard.
fixed: The final FIPS 204 (August 2024) sets ML-DSA-65 signatures at 3,309 bytes and ML-DSA-87 at 4,627 bytes; the entry now gives those figures.

title: P2PK (Pay to Public Key)
wrong: The entry said P2PK was mostly abandoned by about 2010 because P2PKH 'replaced it for new receives once the community recognized that revealing the public key only at spend time was strictly better', presenting hashed addresses as a later invention.
fixed: Both script types shipped in Bitcoin's first release; Satoshi's code calls P2PKH the 'short account number' form. The original client used P2PK for coinbase rewards, pay-to-IP payments and its own change, and P2PK's share of new outputs fell from 99.5% in 2009 to 30% in 2010 and 2.5% in 2011 as coins changed hands by address.

title: P2PKH (Pay to Public Key Hash)
wrong: The entry said P2PKH replaced 'the older P2PK format around 2010' and compared its 20-byte hash with 'a public key's 33 bytes'.
fixed: P2PK is not older: both formats shipped in Bitcoin's first release, and P2PKH overtook P2PK during 2010 as coins began changing hands by address. Public keys of that era were 65 bytes; the 33-byte compressed form came later, with Bitcoin 0.6.0.

title: P2WSH (Pay to Witness Script Hash)
wrong: The entry said new multisig wallets 'typically default to Taproot in 2026'.
fixed: BIP 48, the multisig derivation standard, still recommends P2WSH as the default; Bitcoin Core only added MuSig2 descriptors in version 30.0 (October 2025) and MuSig2 signing in version 31.0 (April 2026); and in September 2026 P2WSH spends were 2.1% of inputs against 0.8% for Taproot script-path spends. The entry now says Taproot multisig is arriving rather than arrived.

title: Post-Quantum Bitcoin
wrong: The entry said that under BIP 361's Phase B Satoshi's P2PK outputs become unspendable without a seed-based rescue, and that anyone who cannot produce a BIP 32 derivation proof, Satoshi included, has their coins locked, implying such a rescue exists for P2PK coins.
fixed: BIP 361's rescue example is a BIP 32 hardened-derivation proof, which only wallets that derive keys from a seed can give. The BIP says no rescue protocol is currently believed possible for P2PK outputs and points to a separate Hourglass proposal for them; under BIP 361 alone those coins are locked.

title: Schnorr Signature
wrong: The entry said that the sum of two valid Schnorr signatures is itself a valid signature for the sum of the corresponding keys.
fixed: Two independently made signatures do not add, because each one's challenge hash commits to its own nonce. What BIP-340 describes is that collaborating signers can produce one signature that is valid for the sum of their public keys, which is what the entry now says.

title: SLH-DSA / SPHINCS+ (FIPS 205)
wrong: The entry said the small and fast SLH-DSA variants trade signature size for verification speed, and that the smallest SLH-DSA signatures are about ten times larger than ML-DSA signatures.
fixed: FIPS 205 defines the s parameter sets for relatively small signatures and the f sets for relatively fast signature generation; verification speed is not the trade. The smallest SLH-DSA signature, 7,856 bytes, is about three times ML-DSA-44's 2,420 bytes.

title: SLH-DSA / SPHINCS+ (FIPS 205)
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin's post-quantum discussion treats SLH-DSA as the conservative fallback and tends to assume ML-DSA as the default scheme.
fixed: That is NIST's ordering, not Bitcoin's. Most Bitcoin post-quantum work has gone into hash-based signatures, whose security rests only on the hash function holding and which are simpler to implement, including the SHRINCS draft BIP posted in August 2026.

title: Address
wrong: The entry said every address encodes a hash of a public key or script, and that the bc1p Taproot format was introduced with BIP 341.
fixed: A Taproot address encodes a tweaked 32-byte public key directly, not a hash. BIP 341 defines the output; the bc1p address encoding is Bech32m from BIP 350.

title: Address Derivation Path
wrong: The entry said some wallets reserve change index 2 for internal change, and called the second path level a registered chain ID.
fixed: BIP 44 defines two chains only: 0, the external chain for receiving addresses, and 1, the internal chain for change. The second level is the registered coin type, 0 for Bitcoin and 1 for testnet.

title: Altcoin
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin borrowed Schnorr signatures and MAST from altcoin research.
fixed: Neither came from an altcoin: Schnorr signatures go back to Claus Schnorr's 1990 patent filing, and Taproot's script trees descend from Bitcoin's own MAST proposals, which BIP 341 lists among the earlier Bitcoin ideas it combines.

title: BIP (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal)
wrong: The entry listed the BIP types as Standards Track, Informational and Process while also saying BIP 3 had replaced the old process in January 2026.
fixed: Since BIP 3 took effect in January 2026 the types are Specification, Informational and Process; Standards Track was the BIP 2 name for what is now a Specification BIP, and it covers interoperability standards such as address formats as well as protocol rules.

title: Bitcoin Core
wrong: The entry said Lurking Wife Mode was added to Bitcoin Core by Sjors Provoost in 2015, and that major versions brought SegWit in 2017 and Taproot signaling in 2021.
fixed: The GUI's Mask Values toggle was written by Hennadii Stepanov and merged in May 2020 (pull request 16432); the Lurking Wife Mode name came from Wasabi Wallet. SegWit's mainnet parameters shipped in the maintenance release 0.13.1 and Taproot's activation parameters in 0.21.1; Bitcoin Core's stated policy is to ship consensus changes first in maintenance releases rather than major versions.

title: Bitcoin Inheritance Planning
wrong: The entry described the time-locked multisig approach as a 2-of-3 in which you hold two keys and a designated heir or trustee holds one, with a time-locked branch letting 'the heir + trustee' spend after a delay. The key counts did not add up and no mechanism was named.
fixed: It now describes a script with a second branch that a designated heir, alone or with a trustee, can use only after the coins have sat untouched for a set delay, enforced by a relative locktime (BIP 68) that CheckSequenceVerify (BIP 112) checks in the script, whose clock restarts whenever the owner moves the coins, and notes that Bitcoin Core's output descriptor language expresses the delay with Miniscript's older().

title: Block Height
wrong: The entry said soft forks such as Taproot, SegWit and BIP 66 activate when a target height is reached or when signaling thresholds clear in a retarget window.
fixed: BIP 66, like BIP 34 and BIP 65, activated by a rolling supermajority of the previous 1,000 blocks, not by a retarget-window tally or a set height. The retarget-period tally is BIP 9's mechanism, used for SegWit, and Taproot's fixed minimum activation height of 709,632 was an addition to it.

title: Block Propagation
wrong: The entry said that in 2026 a new block typically reaches about 80% of reachable nodes within 5-8 seconds and substantially everyone within 30 seconds, and listed Falcon alongside FIBRE as dedicated relay networks run by miners that push blocks across the globe in tens of milliseconds.
fixed: No measurement supports those figures. The KIT network monitor, which records when its peers in Germany announce a new block, saw half of the announcements within about 0.8 seconds of the first and 90% within about 2.5 seconds in October 2026; the 2013 measurement across the reachable network (median 6.5 seconds) is given for comparison. Falcon was removed, since its site no longer exists, and the FIBRE description now follows the FIBRE project's own page, which says the original network sat in stasis for almost a decade before a public network was revived.

title: Dust
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core won't relay a transaction with an output below its dust threshold at all.
fixed: Since Bitcoin Core 29.0 there is one exception, ephemeral dust: a zero-fee transaction may carry one dust output if a child transaction relayed with it spends that output. The 546-sat figure for a legacy output was right; the entry now also gives the P2WPKH figure, 294 sats at the default 3 sat/vB dust fee rate, and calls the policy by its glossary name, the dust limit.

title: Genesis Block
wrong: The entry said the genesis message was written in 80 bytes, implied that Satoshi deliberately hard-coded the 50 BTC reward so that it is not part of the UTXO set, and said its author had not been seen since the block was mined.
fixed: The headline in the coinbase is 69 bytes; 80 bytes is the size of a block header. The reward is unspendable because the original code never added the genesis coinbase to the UTXO set, a special case Bitcoin Core preserves, and whether Satoshi intended it is not known. Satoshi kept posting publicly until December 2010.

title: HTLC (Hashed Time-Locked Contract)
wrong: The entry said an HTLC's funds are spendable by anyone who reveals the preimage, and its script sketch showed a claim path with no signature check.
fixed: The claim path is bound to the intended receiver's key as well as the preimage; a revealed preimage alone identifies nobody, so without the signature check anyone who saw it could take the funds. The script sketch now shows the receiver's signature on the claim path and the sender's on the refund path.

title: Key Split
wrong: The entry said SLIP-39 is a standardized Shamir scheme for BIP 39 seeds, and that tools like SeedSigner can produce SLIP-39 shares from any seed.
fixed: SLIP-39 splits a wallet's BIP 32 master seed using its own 1024-word list and was proposed by the BIP 39 authors as a replacement for BIP 39; the two are mostly not compatible, and converting an existing phrase yields 59-word shares. SeedSigner's published feature list does not include SLIP-39, so that claim was removed.

title: KYC (Know Your Customer)
wrong: The entry said every exchange hacked since 2014 has leaked KYC data including passport scans and home addresses to attackers who use it for physical attacks, and it listed submarine swaps among non-KYC ways to obtain bitcoin.
fixed: The blanket claim was replaced with a sourced example: Coinbase's May 2025 disclosure that bribed support agents had handed attackers customer names, addresses, partial Social Security numbers, government ID images and balances, used in social-engineering thefts. Submarine swaps exchange on-chain bitcoin for Lightning bitcoin and are not a way to acquire bitcoin, so they were removed; the named marketplaces were replaced with FinCEN's own line between users and money transmitters.

title: Layer 1
wrong: The entry said layer 1 handles about 7 transactions per second on average with a hard cap that doesn't change, and that layer 1 is the part of Bitcoin that doesn't change.
fixed: The consensus cap is 4,000,000 weight units per block, not a transaction count; yearly averages since 2016 have ranged from about 2.5 to 7 transactions per second depending on transaction size. Layer 1's rules do change, by soft fork, with SegWit and Taproot as the landmark examples.

title: Merkle Root
wrong: The entry said the Merkle root is a 32-byte commitment to potentially gigabytes of transaction data.
fixed: A block is capped at 4,000,000 weight units, under 4 MB serialized, so a Merkle root commits to at most a few megabytes of transaction data. The sentence now says so.

title: Miner
wrong: The entry said, in the present tense, that today's miners sit near hydro in Sichuan during the wet season, stranded gas in West Texas, geothermal in Iceland and off-peak nuclear in France.
fixed: China clamped down on mining in 2021, so the Sichuan example is now dated to when China still allowed mining. The Texas, Iceland and France examples had no source and were replaced with the siting patterns the Cambridge Digital Mining Industry Report documents: hydro-rich regions, flared gas at oil wells and stranded renewables.

title: Not Your Keys, Not Your Coins
wrong: The entry dated QuadrigaCX's failure to 2018.
fixed: Quadriga's CEO died in December 2018, but the exchange announced the death on January 14, 2019 and had ceased operations and filed for creditor protection by February 5, 2019. The collapse is now dated 2019, matching the QuadrigaCX entry and the custody chapter.

title: Paper Wallet
wrong: The entry said a paper wallet has to be swept whole because Bitcoin Script doesn't allow partial spends of a UTXO, and that most paper-wallet losses come from people sending change to nowhere.
fixed: A transaction spends a UTXO in full whatever the script; the remainder goes to a change output controlled by the wallet that signed. The classic loss is spending part of a paper wallet from a software wallet and assuming the rest is still on the paper, when it sits at a change address that was never backed up.

title: Payment Channel
wrong: The entry said payments inside a channel are enforced cryptographically rather than via the proof-of-work chain.
fixed: Channel states are enforced by the chain: either party can broadcast the latest signed state at any time, and in Lightning a party that broadcasts a revoked state forfeits the channel balance to the other side through a penalty transaction. The chain is the court of last resort, not bypassed.

title: Price Floor (BTC)
wrong: The 2024 bullet said hash rate growth merely slowed after the April 2024 halving and that price did not crash because spot demand had structural ETF support, stated as fact without a source.
fixed: Hash rate fell after the halving: difficulty dropped about 10 percent between April 24 and July 5, 2024 before resuming growth. The ETF explanation was unsupported and was replaced by what the data show, a price between about $50,000 and $73,000 through October 2024 rather than a fall toward the new cost of production.

title: Proof-of-Work (PoW)
wrong: The entry said producing a valid block hash takes trillions of attempts.
fixed: The expected number of attempts is the difficulty times 2^32, roughly 570 sextillion (5.7 x 10^23) at the October 2026 difficulty of about 133 trillion.

title: Public Key
wrong: The entry said most address types hash the public key with SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160 'or just SHA-256 for newer formats', and that the public key is only revealed when you spend.
fixed: Legacy and native SegWit single-key addresses both use HASH160 (SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160); the SHA-256-only form hashes a script, not a key; and Taproot addresses contain a tweaked public key directly, so the hashing protection against a future quantum attack does not apply to them.

title: Reorg (Reorganization)
wrong: The entry called the 25-block reorganization of March 2013 the deepest a software disagreement has caused on mainnet, said deep reorgs have been caused by brief network partitions or deliberate testnet attacks, and described the abandoned blocks as invalidated.
fixed: The 53-block reorganization of 16 August 2010, when the patched chain overtook the chain carrying the value overflow block, was deeper; the entry now names both, drops the unsupported causes, and calls the abandoned blocks stale, which is what they are.

title: Replace-by-Fee (RBF)
wrong: The entry said a transaction signals replaceability with an nSequence value below the maximum, that only nodes following BIP 125 replace transactions, and that merchants accepting zero-conf payments could require non-RBF transactions instead of waiting for a confirmation.
fixed: The signal is an nSequence of 0xfffffffd or lower (0xfffffffe does not signal); a replacement must also pay for its own relay; and since Bitcoin Core 28.0 (October 2024) nodes replace unsignaled transactions by default, with the option to disable that removed in 29.0, so requiring non-RBF transactions no longer protects anyone.

title: Second Layer
wrong: The entry described Ark as a service operator letting users transact through short-lived off-chain channels, called Chaumian e-cash mints federated, and called Lightning genuinely trustless.
fixed: Ark shares on-chain UTXOs through trees of pre-signed off-chain transactions built in rounds, with expiring virtual UTXOs and unilateral exit; e-cash mints hold the bitcoin and issue blind-signed tokens, and users must trust the mint; Lightning needs no trusted third party but does need someone watching the chain.

title: Tor Hidden Service
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core has shipped first-class Tor support since 2014, that Tor adds about 200 to 500 ms of round-trip time because of a three-hop relay structure, and that Tor's random circuit selection protects a node against eclipse attacks.
fixed: Bitcoin Core has had Tor support since version 0.7 in 2012 and has created onion services automatically since version 0.12 in 2016. A connection to an onion service runs through six relays, three picked by each side, and the Tor Project's own measurements put the median round trip at about 440 ms in 2026, from roughly 290 to 700 ms across its vantage points. The entry now credits eclipse resistance to Bitcoin Core keeping an outbound connection on every reachable network since version 26.0, which its release notes say improves resistance to eclipse attacks.

title: BIP 32 (HD Wallets)
wrong: The entry said BIP 32 starts from one 512-bit seed that is split directly into the master private key and chaincode, and that restoring a BIP 32 seed in any standard wallet gives the same addresses.
fixed: BIP 32 accepts a seed of 128 to 512 bits and runs it through HMAC-SHA512 keyed with the string 'Bitcoin seed'; it is that 512-bit output that is split into the master key and chaincode. The same addresses follow only when both wallets use the same derivation path and script type, because BIP 32 leaves the tree layout advisory.

title: BIP 39 (Mnemonic Seed)
wrong: The entry said the same construction is used by every major modern Bitcoin wallet, and that the checksum catches almost all transcription errors.
fixed: BIP 39 is the most common seed phrase standard but not universal: Electrum deliberately does not generate BIP 39 seeds and uses its own versioned format. The spec describes its checksum as short, with only modest odds of catching random errors; the entry now says it catches most errors and gives the miss rates, about 1 in 16 for 12 words and 1 in 256 for 24.

title: Output Descriptor
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core made descriptor wallets the default in 0.21 (2021) and mandatory for new wallets in 0.22, and that the legacy addmultisigaddress style of wallet management was deprecated.
fixed: Bitcoin Core 0.21 (January 2021) introduced descriptor wallets as an experimental, non-default option; 23.0 (April 2022) made them the default for new wallets; 30.0 (October 2025) removed legacy wallets and the legacy-only RPCs, addmultisigaddress included. There was never a Bitcoin Core 0.22.

title: Shamir's Secret Sharing
wrong: The entry said SLIP-39 is a wordlist-based Shamir scheme for BIP 39 seeds, and that SeedSigner can produce SLIP-39 shares from any seed.
fixed: SLIP-39 splits a wallet's BIP 32 master seed using its own 1024-word list and was proposed by the BIP 39 authors as a replacement for BIP 39; the two are mostly not compatible, and converting an existing phrase yields 59-word shares. SeedSigner's published feature list does not include SLIP-39, so that claim was removed.

title: The Block Size War
wrong: The chapter stated one side's account of SegWit's 2017 activation as fact: that the moment users forced the issue ended the standoff, that the industry acted before the users forced the question on August 1, and that, faced with the flag day, the miners moved and BIP-91 offered them a face-saving exit.
fixed: The order is settled but the credit is disputed. BIP-148 set the August 1 deadline in March 2017, the New York Agreement was signed in May, and BIP-91 made SegWit signaling mandatory from July 23, nine days before the deadline. UASF supporters say the flag day forced miners to signal; the SegWit2x organizers said their agreement broke the deadlock, and BIP-91 was written to make the two plans compatible.

title: Bitcoin Obituaries
wrong: The entry said the block size fight "was settled by the UASF", stating one side's account as fact.
fixed: The fight was settled in 2017, by a UASF deadline of August 1 or by the miners' BIP 91 compromise that made SegWit signaling mandatory nine days before it, depending on whom you ask. UASF supporters credit the deadline; the SegWit2x organizers credited their own agreement.

title: Bitcoin and Energy
wrong: The chapter called a miner "the only industrial-scale electricity buyer" that is location-agnostic, interruptible in seconds and indifferent to when power arrives, called miners "the most flexible load ever connected", said that when power costs more than the bitcoin it would mine a miner "shuts off and resells. No agreement needed; arithmetic does it," and said Riot handed its megawatts back to the grid "in seconds" in August 2023. None of it was sourced.
fixed: A miner is a rare kind of industrial-scale buyer, not the only one: NERC's 2025 review of large loads found that mining and AI facilities can cycle on and off in under a minute and recorded one mining site dropping 298 megawatts in 25 seconds, and a grid can only count on that speed from loads enrolled in a curtailment or demand-response program. A miner can resell the power it is not using only if its contract allows it, as Riot's long-term fixed-price agreement does; a miner buying at the spot price just stops. Riot's filing says it curtailed more than 95 percent of its load during peak-demand periods and gives no timing.

title: Centralized Exchange (CEX)
wrong: The entry said the 2022 contagion alone destroyed tens of billions in customer balances, and grouped Genesis with the 2022 failures without noting that it did not file for bankruptcy until 2023.
fixed: The 2022 contagion locked up billions of dollars of customer balances for years rather than destroying tens of billions: Celsius halted withdrawals with $4.7 billion of customer assets on its platform, and FTX had a shortfall of about $8 billion. Much of that money was later paid back in dollars through the bankruptcies, which the Counterparty Risk entry now covers. Genesis froze its lending business in November 2022 and filed for bankruptcy in January 2023.

title: Counterparty Risk
wrong: The entry said Celsius, BlockFi, Voyager, Genesis and FTX all collapsed inside one year, and that customers who had moved BTC into 'yield' arrangements lost most of it.
fixed: Genesis froze its lending business in November 2022 but did not file for bankruptcy until January 2023. Customer recoveries varied and took years: Voyager's creditors had received 70 percent of their allowed claims by September 2024, Celsius creditors got about 60 percent back in cash and crypto over two distributions in 2024 plus shares in a new mining company, BlockFi announced in 2024 that it would pay customer claims in full, and FTX had paid or set aside 100 percent of every allowed customer claim by July 2026. Claims were fixed in dollars as of the day each platform filed, so depositors missed bitcoin's later rise in price.

title: Decentralization
wrong: The chapter said the mining majority "caved when faced with the potential chain split UASF threatened", stating one side's account of why SegWit activated in 2017 as fact.
fixed: BIP 148 set an August 1, 2017 flag day. Nine days before it, miners made SegWit signaling mandatory among themselves through BIP 91, every block from July 23 on signaled, and the split never came; SegWit activated at block 481,824 on August 24. Whether the flag day forced the miners' hand is disputed: UASF supporters say it did, and the SegWit2x organizers credited their own agreement.

title: Energy FUD
wrong: The entry said mining "can stabilize renewable grids" and that miners turning off in seconds is a grid service "conventional industrial loads can't provide", without a source.
fixed: ERCOT runs programs that use Bitcoin miners as flexible demand, and an enrolled miner can shut off in seconds, which NERC's 2025 review of large loads documents. NERC says the same of AI facilities, so the speed is rare among older industrial loads rather than unique to mining, and whether the payments for it are fair is a separate debate.

title: Loop In/Out
wrong: The entry said Loop offers liquidity management without on-chain cost, put the service fee at typically 0.1 to 0.5 percent, and called Loop the most-deployed submarine swap service.
fixed: Every Loop swap has an on-chain leg that pays a miner fee; what it avoids is opening or closing a channel, and Loop Out batches its on-chain transactions to cut that cost. Lightning Labs publishes no fee range: the server fee is quoted per swap in satoshis, and in their worked example a 1,000,000 sat Loop Out paid 3,260 sat to the server (about 0.3 percent), 6,802 sat on-chain and 2,524 sat in routing fees. The entry now describes Loop as Lightning Labs' own swap tool, bundled with their Lightning Terminal package, rather than the most-deployed service.

title: Miner Signaling
wrong: The entry said SegWit "activated only after" user-activated soft fork pressure "threatened to force the issue" and that "the threat of UASF changed the dynamic", stating one side's account as fact, and it listed no sources.
fixed: SegWit was stuck at about 30% miner support against a 95% threshold. BIP 148 set an August 1, 2017 flag day; miners moved first, making SegWit signaling mandatory among themselves through BIP 91 from July 23, and SegWit locked in on August 9. Whether the flag day forced the miners' hand is disputed: UASF supporters say it did, and the SegWit2x organizers credited their own agreement. The entry now lists its sources.

title: Mining
wrong: The chapter said mining is "uniquely well-suited" as a buyer of last resort, stated as fact that miners switching on and off "stabilizes grids and improves renewables economics", and said Riot earned $31.7 million in August 2023 by switching off for ERCOT, when most of that money came from reselling its contracted power.
fixed: Mining can be switched off in seconds and back on in under a minute, which NERC's 2025 review of large loads documents with one facility shedding 298 megawatts in 25 seconds, and a grid can only count on that from miners enrolled in a curtailment or demand-response program. Riot's $31.7 million in August 2023 was $24.2 million from selling its contracted power back to the grid and $7.4 million in demand-response credits; whether such payments are a public service or a subsidy is left to the energy chapter.

title: Stranded Energy
wrong: The entry called a Bitcoin miner "the only large electricity buyer" that is location-agnostic, interruptible in seconds and indifferent to when power arrives, and said a miner is "uniquely able" to monetize stranded energy, with no source.
fixed: A miner is a rare kind of large electricity buyer with those three properties, not the only one. NERC's 2025 review of large loads says mining and AI facilities can cycle on and off in under a minute and recorded one mining facility dropping 298 megawatts in 25 seconds.

title: Submarine Swap
wrong: The entry said a submarine swap in (on-chain to Lightning) is used to fund inbound liquidity on a Lightning channel, that submarine swaps in general are a clean way to buy inbound liquidity, and listed Lightning-to-Lightning transfers across implementations as a use.
fixed: A swap in moves on-chain coins into your Lightning balance, which adds outbound capacity and uses up room to receive. It is the swap out, Lightning to on-chain, that frees inbound capacity. A submarine swap always has one on-chain leg and one Lightning leg, so it is not a Lightning-to-Lightning transfer; the entry now states the direction for each swap, describes peer-to-peer rebalancing with PeerSwap in place of the dropped use, and cites Lightning Labs' Loop docs, the PeerSwap spec and the Boltz docs.

title: Quantum and Bitcoin
wrong: The chapter said the Patoshi miner's blocks account for roughly 22 percent of Bitcoin's first year, a figure taken from a ChainQuery story that ChainQuery has since corrected.
fixed: Sergio Demian Lerner's count puts the Patoshi pattern at about 40 percent of the first 50,000 blocks, which is what ChainQuery's corrected story and the chapter now say.

title: Atomic Swap Refill
wrong: The entry said atomic swap refill let a routing node move balance between two of its channels through a swap with another node, restoring routing capacity without an on-chain transaction, and it described the technique as shifting channel capacity.
fixed: The swaps it covers, such as Loop In, Loop Out and PeerSwap, need on-chain transactions, on Bitcoin or, with PeerSwap, on Liquid; PeerSwap's protocol uses two per swap. They move balance from one side of a channel to the other, and the channel's total capacity stays the same. One way to rebalance that does stay off-chain is a circular payment to yourself through other nodes.

title: BIP 148 (UASF)
wrong: The entry said BIP-148 ended a multi-year SegWit activation deadlock that had persisted for over a year.
fixed: Miners could signal for SegWit from November 15, 2016, and BIP-91 made every block signal from July 23, 2017, so the deadlock lasted about eight months. In May and early June 2017, only about 30 percent of blocks signaled for SegWit.

title: BIP 9 (VersionBits)
wrong: The entry said a significant minority of miners refused to signal for SegWit in 2017, and listed the BIP-8 proposal as coming after BIP-148 and BIP-91.
fixed: In May and early June 2017, only about 30 percent of blocks signaled for SegWit, far short of the 95 percent it needed, so the miners holding out were a majority. BIP-8 was proposed in February 2017, before BIP-148 and BIP-91.

title: BIP 91
wrong: The entry said BIP-91 lowered SegWit's activation threshold to 80%.
fixed: BIP-91 was a separate deployment with its own 80% threshold, on bit 4. It made SegWit signaling mandatory, but SegWit's own 95% threshold never changed, and every block in the period before SegWit's lock-in signaled for it.

title: Bitcoin Governance
wrong: The entry listed BIP-148, the 2017 user-activated soft fork, among proposed changes that failed.
fixed: BIP-148's rule, that blocks signal for SegWit from August 1, 2017, was already being met when that date came: every block from July 23 until SegWit locked in signaled for it. SegWit activated on August 24, 2017.

title: Block Size War
wrong: The entry said miners activated SegWit through BIP-91 in July 2017.
fixed: Only BIP-91 took effect in July: it locked in on July 21 and was enforced from block 477,120 on July 23, 2017, so every block signaled for SegWit before the August 1 flag day. SegWit itself locked in on August 9 and activated at block 481,824 on August 24.

title: Celsius, Genesis, and 3AC (the 2022 Contagion)
wrong: The entry presented Celsius's June 2022 withdrawal freeze as a result of Three Arrows Capital's default, and said BlockFi went down the same way as the lenders 3AC failed to repay.
fixed: Celsius froze withdrawals on 12 June 2022, before 3AC was put into liquidation at the end of that month. BlockFi was hurt by 3AC's collapse but kept going on a $400 million credit line from FTX, and filed for bankruptcy after FTX failed in November 2022.

title: Chain Flag Day
wrong: The entry said SegWit activated via BIP-91 a week before BIP-148's August 1, 2017 flag day.
fixed: BIP-91 was enforced from block 477,120 on July 23, 2017, about nine days before the flag day, and every block from then until SegWit locked in on August 9 signaled for SegWit. SegWit itself activated at block 481,824 on August 24, 2017.

title: Deployment Threshold (Soft Fork)
wrong: The entry said BIP 91 lowered SegWit's signaling threshold to 80% with a forced lock-in, that BIP 148 showed nodes could enforce SegWit rules even without miner signaling, and that ASICBoost was incompatible with SegWit.
fixed: BIP 91 ran its own 80% deployment on bit 4 and, once active from block 477,120 on July 23, 2017, rejected blocks that did not signal for SegWit. SegWit's 95% threshold never changed and was met by 2,016 of 2,016 blocks. BIP 148 required signaling from August 1 and was never tested. Only a covert form of ASICBoost conflicted with SegWit.

title: Escrow
wrong: The entry said Bisq uses 2-of-3 multisig escrow with an arbitrator, that an HTLC seller reveals the preimage after delivering the goods, and that script-based escrow costs nothing beyond transaction fees. It also named RoboSats as an example after saying the escrow agent never holds the funds.
fixed: Bisq locks each trade in a 2-of-2 multisig with both traders' deposits, and its mediators hold no key. An HTLC pays the seller for revealing a secret and cannot check whether any goods arrived. Bisq and Hodl Hodl charge trading fees. On RoboSats the coordinator node settles the seller's hold invoice, briefly holds the funds while paying the buyer, and its staff decide disputes.

title: FTX
wrong: The entry said FTX, Alameda and roughly 130 affiliated companies filed for bankruptcy on 11 November 2022, and that Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted on seven fraud counts.
fixed: The court record shows FTX Trading and 101 affiliated companies filing on 11 and 14 November 2022. Bankman-Fried was convicted on all seven counts against him, including fraud and conspiracy to launder money.

title: Peg-out
wrong: The entry described a Liquid peg-out as the user burning L-BTC, as if anyone could peg out directly.
fixed: On Liquid, only federation members holding a peg-out authorization key can peg out, and other users go through one of them.

title: The BIP Process
wrong: The chapter said a minority of miners held SegWit back by declining to signal, and that miners began signaling weeks before BIP-148's August 1, 2017 deadline.
fixed: Most blocks did not signal. Signaling had been open since November 2016, and in May and early June 2017 only about 30 percent of blocks signaled for SegWit, against the 95 percent it needed. Every block signaled from July 23, about nine days before the deadline, once the BIP-91 deployment took effect.

title: The Block Size War
wrong: The chapter said BIP-91 got SegWit activated before BIP-148's August 1, 2017 deadline and went into force around July 20, and a figure description said mandatory SegWit signaling began that day. It also implied SegWit had activated before Bitcoin Cash split off on August 1. Its timeline figure also dated mandatory signaling to July 20, and its countdown figure said that left 12 days to spare before the flag day.
fixed: BIP-91 locked in on the evening of July 20, 2017, US time (July 21 UTC), and was enforced from block 477,120 on July 23, so every block signaled for SegWit before August 1. SegWit itself locked in on August 9 and activated at block 481,824 on August 24, after Bitcoin Cash split off. Mandatory signaling began about nine days before the flag day, and both figures now say so.

title: Voyager Digital
wrong: The entry said Voyager's "FDIC insured" line was technically accurate, and that customers who relied on it had simply misread what was being promised.
fixed: The Federal Trade Commission charged that telling customers "YOUR USD IS FDIC INSURED" was false. Voyager was not a bank and its customers' deposits were not eligible for FDIC insurance; their cash was protected only if Voyager's partner bank failed, and their crypto not at all. Voyager settled in 2023, and its former CEO settled in 2025.

title: Balanced Channel (Lightning)
wrong: The entry said submarine swaps such as Loop and PeerSwap effectively move capacity in or out of channels without closing them.
fixed: Submarine swaps trade Lightning balance for on-chain bitcoin without closing the channel. They shift balance from one side of the channel to the other, and the channel's total capacity stays the same. Splicing is what changes the size of the channel itself.

title: BIP 91
wrong: The entry said SegWit activated about 10 days before BIP-148's August 1, 2017 deadline, and that BIP-91 locked in in mid-July and activated in August. It also described the miners holding out as a minority who had refused for over a year.
fixed: BIP-91 locked in on July 21, 2017 and went live at block 477,120 on July 23, and every block from then until SegWit locked in signaled for it. SegWit itself locked in on August 9 and activated at block 481,824 on August 24. Signaling for SegWit had been open since November 2016, and the SegWit2x organizers put miner support at only 30% in May 2017.

title: Bitcoin and Energy
wrong: The chapter's chart put gold mining's electricity use at 132 to 265 TWh a year and said Bitcoin fell inside that range. It said environmental groups called Riot's $31.7 million in grid payments "paying a polluter not to pollute," and called the best-known e-waste estimate "as much as the Netherlands."
fixed: The chart shows gold mining at about 131 TWh, Cambridge's 2019 estimate, which counts all the energy gold mines use, diesel included, so Bitcoin sits a little above it. A KVUE report quotes Environment Texas's director calling the payment absurd and asking that households be paid to conserve instead. The e-waste study compared its figure with the Netherlands' small IT equipment waste.

title: Bloom Filter
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core's Bloom filter service first became opt-in and was later disabled by default in v0.19. It also called Bloom filters a historical artifact in Bitcoin.
fixed: Bitcoin Core served Bloom filters by default, with a -peerbloomfilters setting to switch them off, until version 0.19.0.1 (November 2019) made off the default. As of October 2026 it is still off by default and can be turned back on. Core also uses Bloom filters internally to track which transactions and addresses each peer already knows.

title: Custodial Wallet
wrong: The entry said QuadrigaCX lost the keys with its CEO in 2019.
fixed: In early 2019 Quadriga told a court that only its CEO, who died in December 2018, could open its cold wallets. The court-appointed monitor found those wallets had been empty since April 2018, and the Ontario Securities Commission concluded that Quadriga had operated like a Ponzi scheme.

title: Decentralized Exchange (DEX)
wrong: The entry said RoboSats escrow is held by a Lightning HTLC, not by the platform.
fixed: The RoboSats seller locks the bitcoin with a Lightning hold invoice to the coordinator's node. When the seller confirms the fiat arrived, the coordinator settles it and briefly holds the funds while paying the buyer. If the trade goes wrong, RoboSats staff decide who gets the escrow.

title: ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund)
wrong: The entry said eleven spot Bitcoin ETFs launched simultaneously in January 2024 and called SPY still the largest ETF in the world.
fixed: The SEC approved eleven spot Bitcoin ETFs on January 10, 2024, but one of them, Hashdex's DEFI, held bitcoin futures until March 27, 2024, when it switched to spot bitcoin. SPY, listed in January 1993, was the first US ETF.

title: Exchange
wrong: The entry said QuadrigaCX's CEO died, or "died", with the only access to its cold wallets, presenting the company's account as fact and hinting that the death was faked.
fixed: After CEO Gerald Cotten died in December 2018, Quadriga said only he could reach its cold wallets. The court-appointed monitor found them empty since April 2018, the Ontario Securities Commission concluded the exchange had operated like a Ponzi scheme, and clients lost at least CAD 169 million.

title: Fee Estimation
wrong: The entry said that in low-traffic periods the fee estimator often returns 1 sat/vB for every target, and called that rate the relay minimum.
fixed: Bitcoin Core 29.1 (September 2025) lowered the default relay minimum to 0.1 sat/vB, and 31.0 (April 2026) lowered the fee estimator's minimum from 1 sat/vB to 0.1 to match. When Core's own wallet picks a fee from its estimates, it still won't go below 1 sat/vB unless its -mintxfee setting is lowered.

title: Fee Floor
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core's default minimum fee rate for accepting a transaction was 1 sat/vB, that the market floor equals that minimum in quiet periods, and that the cheapest mined transactions paid 1 to 2 sat/vB in low-traffic times from 2024 to 2026.
fixed: Bitcoin Core's default relay minimum was 1 sat/vB until version 29.1 (September 2025) lowered it to 0.1 sat/vB, and each node operator can change it. In quiet periods the floor can drop below 1 sat/vB: block 970,789, mined on October 10, 2026, had a median fee rate of about 0.28 sat/vB.

title: Inactive Channel
wrong: The entry listed marking an inactive channel as private as one of the things an operator can do with it.
fixed: Whether a channel is private is settled when it opens. A public channel can't be switched to private later; the only way is to close it and open a new one. A private channel to a mobile wallet or payment-only node can sit idle for long stretches and still be worth keeping.

title: Low-S Signatures
wrong: The entry said low-S became relay policy through BIP 146 and a consensus rule for SegWit inputs through BIP 141, and that it left exactly one valid signature per key and message. Its title also called low-S the rule that killed ECDSA malleability.
fixed: Bitcoin Core has enforced low-S as relay policy since version 0.11.1 (October 2015), and it never became a consensus rule: BIP 146, which proposed that, was closed, and BIP 141 has no low-S rule. The key holder can still make other valid signatures. SegWit is what fixed third-party malleability.

title: Mt. Gox to FTX: The Custody Graveyard
wrong: The chapter said every word of Voyager's "FDIC insured" marketing was technically accurate. Its timeline figure put Genesis's loans to 3AC at about $3.5 billion or more, and said about 850,000 BTC were stolen from Mt. Gox.
fixed: The Federal Trade Commission charged that telling customers their accounts were FDIC insured was false, and Voyager settled. The insurance covered only the US dollars Voyager kept at a partner bank, and only if that bank failed. Genesis's own bankruptcy filing puts its loans to 3AC at about $2.4 billion, and the figure now says so. About 850,000 BTC went missing from Mt. Gox, but 200,000 were later found in an old wallet, so the figure no longer calls them all stolen.

title: Mt. Gox to FTX: The Custody Graveyard
wrong: The chapter said customers lost money in every one of the seven collapses, told the 2022 story as if Three Arrows Capital's default set off Celsius's freeze, said about 130 companies filed for bankruptcy with FTX, and said Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted on seven fraud counts.
fixed: In most of the collapses customers lost some money for good. Celsius froze withdrawals on 12 June 2022, before 3AC was put into liquidation at the end of that month. FTX, Alameda and about 100 related companies filed for bankruptcy, and Bankman-Fried was convicted on all seven counts, including fraud and conspiracy to launder money.

title: Node
wrong: The entry said the network had roughly 15,000 to 20,000 publicly reachable full nodes, and that the block headers a light SPV wallet downloads come to a few megabytes.
fixed: bitnodes.io counted 25,514 reachable nodes on October 9, 2026, including 1,829 Knots nodes that no longer follow Bitcoin's main chain, and one estimate put the total at about 104,000. Each block header is 80 bytes, so the headers for the roughly 970,000 blocks mined by October 2026 come to about 78 MB.

title: OP_RETURN
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Knots keeps the 80-byte OP_RETURN default and applies it to other ways of embedding data as well. It did not say that newer Knots releases had left Bitcoin's main chain.
fixed: Knots relayed only 40 bytes of OP_RETURN data for years, until a November 2025 release raised that to 80. By default it won't relay transactions that carry data outside OP_RETURN outputs, such as inscriptions. Nodes running Knots releases from May 9, 2026 on left Bitcoin's main chain in August 2026.

title: Peg-in
wrong: The entry said sidechain tokens are economically indistinguishable from BTC, with 1 L-BTC equal to 1 BTC, without saying that this depends on the peg working.
fixed: Each sidechain token is meant to be redeemable for one BTC, but only while the peg works. On Liquid, peg-outs were halted after an exploit on September 6, 2026. As of October 10, 2026 they were still paused, and the peg wallet held about 600 BTC less than the L-BTC in circulation.

title: Premium / Discount (to NAV)
wrong: The entry called pre-2024 GBTC a closed-end trust with a fixed share count and no creation of shares, and said buyers faced a six-month lockup from 2017 on. It also blamed the February 2021 collapse of the premium partly on US futures ETFs that launched in October 2021.
fixed: Before January 2024, GBTC sold new shares to accredited investors in private placements at prices based on NAV. Buyers had to hold them for a year, and for six months once the trust had been an SEC reporting company for 90 days. With redemptions suspended since 2014, its price closed as much as 142% above NAV and 49% below.

title: Rug Pull
wrong: The entry listed Mt. Gox among custodial scams in which the operator drains customers' funds, saying the custodian was the scam.
fixed: Investigators traced Mt. Gox's missing coins to thefts from its hot wallet, and its CEO was acquitted of embezzlement, so it fits that pattern less well than QuadrigaCX, Bitconnect and BitClub Network, which regulators or prosecutors described as frauds or Ponzi schemes.

title: Sidechain
wrong: The entry said that on a sidechain you can reverse the peg at any time to redeem your BTC, with Liquid as its main example. It also listed statechains (Mercury Layer) among notable Bitcoin sidechains.
fixed: Whether you can reverse the peg yourself, and when, depends on who runs it. On Liquid, only federation members holding a peg-out authorization key can peg out, so other users go through one of them, and peg-outs were halted after an exploit on September 6, 2026 and still paused as of October 10, 2026. Statechains, an offchain system, are no longer listed.

title: Signature Clipping
wrong: The entry said low-S was a consensus rule for SegWit under BIP 141, that the DER standard itself allowed several encodings of one signature, that BIP 66 only made the extras non-standard, and that malleability was solved for all new transactions.
fixed: DER allows one encoding; the extra forms came from OpenSSL accepting non-DER signatures, and BIP 66 made strict DER a consensus rule in July 2015. Low-S is only Bitcoin Core relay policy and SegWit has no low-S rule, so a miner could still confirm a high-S copy of a transaction that spends older, non-SegWit outputs.

title: Spot Bitcoin ETF
wrong: The entry said approval came after eleven years of rejections, starting with a Winklevoss application rejected in 2013, and quoted the SEC as repeatedly citing "manipulation in the underlying market".
fixed: The Winklevoss Bitcoin Trust filed with the SEC in July 2013, and the SEC first turned down its exchange listing in March 2017. By Chair Gensler's count, the SEC disapproved more than 20 spot bitcoin filings from 2018 through March 2023. The orders turned on the Exchange Act requirement that an exchange's rules be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices.

title: Node Autoban
wrong: The entry described Bitcoin Core as still scoring misbehaving peers and banning their IP addresses for 24 hours at 100 points. It said consensus-invalid transactions earned a small, additive score, listed repeated or nonexistent data requests as offenses, said bans can be extended if abuse persists, and said the system makes denial-of-service attacks expensive.
fixed: Automatic bans ended with 0.20.1 in 2020, when discouragement replaced them, and 28.0 (2024) dropped the score, so one offense means disconnection and discouragement. Under the old system a consensus-invalid transaction cost the full 100 points, and since 30.0 it is not punished at all. Bans are set only by hand, and Bitcoin Core's code says neither bans nor discouragement protect against denial of service.

title: Peer Bookmark
wrong: The entry told readers to combine -addnode or -connect with the -whitelist setting to exempt those peers from rate limits and ban scoring, and said this pairing avoids default policy throttles.
fixed: By default -whitelist applies only to incoming connections, so it does nothing for peers added with -addnode or -connect unless its out flag is set. Those peers are already never disconnected or discouraged for misbehavior, and current Bitcoin Core has no ban score.

title: Peer Management
wrong: The entry said a misbehaving peer's score rises until it triggers disconnection and a temporary ban, and that autoban kicks in for repeated invalid data or spam. It also said Bitcoin Core picks outbound peers from different ASNs using a bundled asmap file, and from different geographies.
fixed: There is no score or automatic ban: a peer that breaks certain protocol rules is disconnected after one offense and its address discouraged, and bans are set only by hand. Outbound peers are limited to one per address group (/16 for IPv4) and spread across reachable networks. Grouping by network operator needs -asmap, which stays off by default even though 31.0 embeds the map, and nothing selects peers by geography.

title: Bitcoin Client
wrong: The entry described Bitcoin Knots as consensus-compatible with Bitcoin Core.
fixed: Knots releases up to May 8, 2026 do not include BIP-110, a temporary limit on data in transactions. Releases from May 9, 2026 on enforce it, and nodes running them left Bitcoin's main chain on August 8, 2026. In September 2026 Knots shipped a hard fork that moved that chain to a BLAKE2b proof of work.

title: Bitcoin Knots
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Knots is consensus-compatible with Bitcoin Core, so a Knots node sees the same chain and accepts the same blocks, and that the two differ only in relay policy.
fixed: Knots releases up to 29.3.knots20260507 (May 8, 2026, UTC) follow the same chain as Core. Releases from 29.3.knots20260508 (May 9, 2026, UTC) on enforce BIP-110, a temporary limit on data in transactions, and nodes running them rejected the main chain's blocks from August 8, 2026 and split off. Knots 29.4.1, released September 2, 2026, is a hard fork that gives that chain a BLAKE2b proof of work.

title: Decentralization
wrong: The chapter called Bitcoin Knots an independent implementation of Bitcoin, alongside btcd and Libbitcoin, and its metrics table counted Knots among "4+" independent clients.
fixed: Knots began as a modified version of Bitcoin Core, merging in Core's code for each release. Its releases from May 9, 2026 on enforce BIP-110, a temporary limit on data in transactions, and nodes running them left Bitcoin's main chain on August 8, 2026. A September 2026 release moved that chain to a different proof of work. btcd and Libbitcoin are the separately written implementations.

title: Fork Watcher
wrong: The entry said forkmonitor.info runs Bitcoin Knots and libbitcoin nodes alongside Bitcoin Core and btcd, and publishes alerts to RSS, Twitter and mailing-list feeds.
fixed: As of October 2026 the site runs several versions of Bitcoin Core plus btcd and bcoin, compares the chains they follow, and keeps a list of stale blocks. It names Localhost Research as its sponsor.

title: Full Node
wrong: The entry said full nodes almost always run Bitcoin Core and offered Bitcoin Knots as an alternative, without saying that newer Knots releases no longer follow Bitcoin's main chain.
fixed: Bitcoin Core runs on most nodes, about 87% in one October 2026 estimate. Knots releases from May 9, 2026 on enforce BIP-110, a temporary limit on data in transactions, and nodes running them left Bitcoin's main chain on August 8, 2026.

title: Node Operator
wrong: The entry listed Bitcoin Knots alongside Bitcoin Core and btcd as software you can download to run a Bitcoin full node.
fixed: Only Knots releases made before May 9, 2026 run on Bitcoin's main chain. Later releases enforce BIP-110, a temporary limit on data in transactions, and nodes running them left the main chain on August 8, 2026.

title: Resource Exhaustion Attack
wrong: The entry said the discard threshold protects nodes from mempool spam by evicting low-fee transactions. It also said Bitcoin Core keeps a ban score and bans peers automatically once their misbehavior adds up, said SegWit's BIP 143 fixed slow quadratic signature hashing outright, and listed limits on chains of unconfirmed transactions as a protocol rule.
fixed: Each node's mempool has a size cap, 300 MB by default in Bitcoin Core. When it is full, the node evicts the lowest-fee-rate transactions and raises its minimum fee. Bitcoin Core keeps no ban score: a peer that breaks certain rules is disconnected and its address discouraged, and bans are set only by hand. BIP 143's faster hashing covers only SegWit inputs, and chain limits are relay policy, not consensus.

title: Authorized Participant
wrong: The entry said custody for 8 of the 11 US spot bitcoin ETFs was at one firm.
fixed: Custody differs by fund and has changed since the 2024 launch, so the entry now gives one documented example: the iShares Bitcoin Trust listed 13 authorized participants in its annual report for 2025, while one custodian, Coinbase Custody, held its bitcoin.

title: Autopilot (Lightning)
wrong: The entry said LND's autopilot tries to rebalance or close channels that are not working out.
fixed: LND's autopilot, which is off by default, only opens channels. It works within a budget, by default up to 60% of the wallet's funds across at most five channels, and its hook for closing a channel does nothing.

title: BIP 66
wrong: The entry said BIP 66 eliminated signature malleability. It also called Mt. Gox the most famous victim of malleability and said malleability was part of the story of the exchange's 850,000 BTC loss.
fixed: BIP 66 left one signature tweak open: flipping a signature's S value gives another valid signature and a new txid, which Bitcoin Core blocks only as relay policy. Mt. Gox blamed malleability in 2014, but a study of more than a year of network data found at most about 386 BTC could have been taken that way.

title: Block Time
wrong: The entry contrasted Bitcoin's 10-minute target with "1 minute like Litecoin" and "15 seconds like Ethereum".
fixed: Litecoin targets 2.5 minutes per block. Ethereum has produced blocks in 12-second slots since the Merge on September 15, 2022, and still did as of October 2026.

title: Discard Threshold
wrong: The entry defined the discard threshold as the minimum fee rate a transaction must pay to stay in a Bitcoin Core node's mempool when memory runs short.
fixed: In Bitcoin Core, the discard threshold is the smallest change output the wallet will create. Smaller change is added to the fee instead. The wallet works it out from its -discardfee rate, 10 sat/vB by default. The mempool's minimum fee is a separate rule.

title: Hal Finney's Running Bitcoin
wrong: The entry said Hal Finney corresponded with Satoshi by email about bugs and improvements through much of 2009.
fixed: Hal's own 2013 account says the emails covered the first few days after he started running Bitcoin in January 2009, mostly him reporting bugs that Satoshi then fixed.

title: Lightning Channel
wrong: The entry said a channel's capacity is fixed at open time and that rebalancing through swap services like Loop In/Out, or splicing, is required for more.
fixed: The funding transaction sets a channel's capacity, split between the two sides. Swap services like Loop In/Out shift that split, refilling or emptying one side, but the total stays the same. Only splicing, which replaces the funding transaction, changes a channel's capacity.

title: Liquid Federation
wrong: The entry said the federation had roughly 65 members, that each member ran a functionary node, and that a malicious majority of the federation could steal the pegged BTC.
fixed: The federation had 87 member companies as of May 2026, but only 15 functionaries, each run by one member, sign blocks and hold the 15 multisig keys to the pegged BTC. Each block and each peg-out needs 11 of the 15 signatures, so in normal operation signing the pegged BTC away would take 11 functionaries colluding or having their keys stolen. A software bug can also drain the peg, as the September 2026 exploit showed.

title: Liquid Network
wrong: The entry described the federation as a consortium of around 65 entities and said a majority of federation members could steal the pegged BTC by signing a malicious peg-out. It also named PAXG, a gold token issued on Ethereum, among the assets issued on Liquid.
fixed: The federation had 87 member companies as of May 2026. Fifteen functionaries, each run by one member, take turns proposing blocks, and each block needs 11 of their 15 signatures. Signing the pegged BTC away would take 11 of those 15 functionaries colluding or having their keys stolen, and a software bug can also drain the peg, as the September 2026 exploit showed. The asset examples are now Tether's USDT, the Brazilian-real stablecoin DePix and tokenized securities.

title: Merkle Block
wrong: The entry said a merkle block message contains the transactions in the block that match the wallet's Bloom filter.
fixed: A merkle block carries the block header and a partial Merkle tree holding the matching transactions' hashes. The full node sends the matching transactions themselves right after it, as separate tx messages.

title: Mt. Gox
wrong: The entry said Mark Karpeles was convicted in 2019 for manipulating data rather than for stealing the coins, and that he was acquitted of stealing them.
fixed: A Tokyo court convicted Karpeles in 2019 of falsifying Mt. Gox's records to inflate its holdings, and acquitted him of the more serious charges, including a charge that he embezzled about $3 million of customers' money.

title: NAV (Net Asset Value)
wrong: The entry listed cash drag, creation cash sitting idle before the fund buys bitcoin, as a contributor to tracking error, and said pre-conversion GBTC had a fixed share count.
fixed: At the iShares Bitcoin Trust, the authorized participant pays for any gap between the price used for NAV and the price the fund pays for bitcoin. Before January 2024, GBTC did issue new shares, in private placements; its gap to NAV lasted because buyers faced a holding period and there was no redemption program.

title: Peg-Guard
wrong: The entry said Liquid's federation members refuse to sign a peg-out if a sidechain bug looks like it is draining the reserve, and that an individual member can refuse to sign and stop a peg-out.
fixed: Liquid has no separate check at peg-out time that the reserve still matches the L-BTC in circulation. The functionaries rely on the sidechain's own validation, and a peg-out needs 11 of 15 functionary signatures, so one refusal cannot block it. In September 2026 a bug let about 3,996 BTC be paid out against unbacked L-BTC.

title: Peg-out
wrong: The entry said that in an SPV-validated peg, sidechain validators approve a peg-out by checking SPV proofs of mainnet activity, and called the design rarely deployed at scale.
fixed: In the SPV peg proposed in the 2014 sidechains paper, Bitcoin itself releases the locked coins when shown an SPV proof that they were sent back on the sidechain. Bitcoin's script cannot check such proofs without a soft fork, so the same paper proposed a federated peg in the meantime.

title: Spot Bitcoin ETF
wrong: The entry presented all eleven funds as spot products that launched on day one, said eight of them held their bitcoin at Coinbase Custody in a concentration not structurally addressed, and called GBTC's 1.50% fee a legacy of its days before conversion.
fixed: Hashdex's DEFI held bitcoin futures until March 27, 2024. In annual reports filed in 2026, Coinbase Custody was a custodian for nine of the eleven but the only one for five, and several funds had added custodians such as Anchorage Digital and BitGo. GBTC's fee was cut from 2.0% to 1.5% when it converted in January 2024.

title: Tracking Error
wrong: The entry listed cash drag as a source of tracking gap, saying creation cash sits idle until the fund buys bitcoin and calling it a real headwind when the price rises. It also said Coinbase Custody held the bitcoin for 8 of the 11 US spot ETFs.
fixed: At the iShares Bitcoin Trust, the authorized participant pays the difference when the fund pays more for bitcoin for a cash creation than the price used for NAV, so a price rise in between does not cost the fund. Custody arrangements differ by fund, so the entry no longer gives a count.

title: Air-gapped
wrong: The entry said a single hardware wallet is air-gapped by design where its keys are concerned, and named Foundation Passport among the devices designed for air-gapped use.
fixed: A hardware wallet used over USB or Bluetooth is not air-gapped, though it still keeps its private keys on the device. Foundation's air-gapped model, Passport Core, is discontinued, and its successor, Passport Prime, is not air-gapped by design.

title: BIP 125 (Replace-by-Fee)
wrong: The entry's list of the five BIP 125 rules left out the rule that the original transaction must signal, and added a higher-feerate rule that BIP 125 does not contain. It also said opt-in RBF was Bitcoin Core's default only through version 23.
fixed: The list now gives BIP 125's own five rules, starting with the signaling rule, and notes where Bitcoin Core has since moved away from them. Opt-in RBF was Core's default from 0.12 (2016) through 27.x, and 28.0 made full RBF the default in 2024.

title: BIP 159
wrong: The entry's summary said BIP 159 proposed a NODE_FILTERS service bit for Bloom or compact filters, and its key points called it filter-related and not widely implemented.
fixed: BIP 159 defines the NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED service bit, which lets a pruned node announce that it serves at least the last 288 blocks. The BIP is marked Deployed, and Bitcoin Core has signaled the bit since version 0.16.0 and connected to such peers since 0.17.0.

title: BIP 66
wrong: The entry said BIP 66 was the first soft fork activated with the BIP 9 miner-signaling mechanism.
fixed: BIP 66 reused the version-number switchover from BIP 34, so once 950 of the previous 1,000 blocks were version 3, version 2 blocks became invalid. BIP 9 came later, and its first deployment was the CSV soft fork of 2016.

title: Bitcoin Dev Kit (BDK)
wrong: The entry listed Mutiny Wallet, which shut down in 2024, and Cake Wallet's Bitcoin module among the notable wallets built on BDK in 2026.
fixed: The examples now come from the list BDK keeps of projects built on it. As of October 2026 that list includes the Bitkey, Proton Wallet, Bull Bitcoin and Liana wallets, Foundation's Envoy app, and infrastructure such as Fedimint and LDK Node. Cake Wallet is not on it.

title: Bitcoin Pizza Day
wrong: The entry said Laszlo Hanyecz posted his offer of 10,000 BTC for two pizzas on May 22, 2010.
fixed: Laszlo Hanyecz posted the offer on the Bitcoin Talk forum on May 18, 2010. Four days later, on May 22, Jeremy Sturdivant (jercos on the forum) took him up on it and had two pizzas delivered.

title: Block Time
wrong: The entry said a block takes over an hour to arrive a few times a year.
fixed: At a 10-minute average, the chance that a block takes over an hour is about 0.25%. That comes to about 130 blocks a year, or two or three a week.

title: Blockchain
wrong: The entry put the chain at about 600 GB, growing by about 150 GB a year.
fixed: The chain held about 775 GB of block data as of October 2026 and grows by roughly 80 GB a year.

title: BOLT
wrong: The entry's example of different Lightning software working together described the Phoenix wallet as running Eclair.
fixed: Phoenix runs on lightning-kmp, a separate ACINQ implementation, so the example now starts with an Eclair node opening a channel to a Core Lightning node.

title: Core Lightning (c-lightning)
wrong: The entry said Eclair powers the Phoenix mobile wallet and is strong on mobile uses, and named Mutiny, which shut down in 2024, as an app built on LDK.
fixed: Eclair is aimed at servers such as routing nodes. ACINQ's mobile wallet runs on lightning-kmp, a separate ACINQ implementation, and the entry's LDK examples are now Cash App and Alby Hub.

title: Decentralization
wrong: The chapter said no single contributor's commits made up more than a few percent of Bitcoin Core's code.
fixed: One developer has written more than a tenth of Bitcoin Core's commits, even with merge commits left out. The chapter now says only that Bitcoin Core has had over a thousand contributors since 2009.

title: Discard Threshold
wrong: The entry said mempool.space's next-block fee estimate shows the discard threshold, and gave about 1 sat/vB as the floor in calm periods.
fixed: mempool.space shows the mempool's fee floor on its dashboard as 'Minimum fee', relabeled 'Purging' when it rises above the relay minimum. Bitcoin Core 29.1 (September 2025) lowered the default relay minimum from 1 to 0.1 sat/vB. The entry's definition was itself corrected on 10 October 2026: in Bitcoin Core the discard threshold is a wallet setting for dropping tiny change, not the mempool floor.

title: Double Spend
wrong: The entry said reversing a payment after six confirmations would take more than half the global hash rate, and that even a sustained majority would succeed only some of the time.
fixed: A smaller attacker can still succeed, with odds that shrink with each confirmation. Meni Rosenfeld's 2012 analysis puts the chance after six confirmations at about 1 in 1,700 for an attacker with 10% of the hash rate and about 1 in 6 for one with 30%. An attacker with more than half is sure to win eventually.

title: Double-Blind Marketplace
wrong: The entry listed AgoraDesk, a peer-to-peer trading site, among the Bitcoin-native double-blind marketplaces running in 2026.
fixed: AgoraDesk wound down in 2024 and its site has been taken offline, so the entry no longer lists it.

title: Elliptic Curve
wrong: The entry listed Taproot, along with P2WPKH, as an address type that keeps the public key hidden until the coins are spent, which gives some protection against a future quantum computer. A caveat added in June 2026 still called Taproot only a partial exception.
fixed: Taproot gives none of that protection, because a Taproot address holds the tweaked public key itself, with no hash in front. The entry now gives P2WPKH as the example of a type that keeps the key hashed until the coins are spent.

title: Fee Bumping
wrong: The entry said RBF requires the original transaction to signal that it can be replaced, with full RBF as an exception, and told senders whose transaction didn't signal to use CPFP or wait.
fixed: Since Bitcoin Core 28.0 (October 2024), Core nodes on default settings run full RBF and accept a replacement whether or not the original signaled. A wallet may still refuse to bump a transaction that didn't signal; Bitcoin Core's own wallet did until 30.0 (October 2025).

title: Fee Rate Escalation
wrong: The entry put the April 2024 fee spike down to the halving, saying fees rose as miners' subsidy income dropped.
fixed: The spike came from the launch of the Runes token protocol, which switched on at block 840,000, the same block as the halving. Two blocks later the median fee rate in mined blocks passed 500 sat/vB, and it stayed above that for nearly 11 hours straight.

title: Fork Detection
wrong: The entry said routine reorgs of one or two blocks happen a few times a year.
fixed: Near-simultaneous block finds leave dozens of stale blocks each year. The public bitcoin-data/stale-blocks dataset counts between 28 and 93 a year from 2022 through 2025, and reorgs two blocks deep are rare.

title: Full Node
wrong: The entry said a full node needs about 600 GB of disk for the chain, growing by about 150 GB a year.
fixed: The chain came to about 775 GB of block data as of October 2026 and grows by roughly 80 GB a year. Bitcoin Core 31's setup screen asks for at least 870 GB.

title: Full RBF
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core made full RBF its default in version 26 (late 2023), and its summary still called full RBF a proposal.
fixed: Bitcoin Core added full RBF as an option in version 24 (late 2022), made it the default in 28.0 (October 2024) and removed the option in 29.0 (April 2025). Every Core node from 29.0 on runs full RBF.

title: Hal Finney's Running Bitcoin
wrong: The entry said Bitcoin Core v0.1 was posted to the cypherpunks mailing list and that Hal Finney received block 70's reward of 10 BTC from Satoshi. It also said his coins, roughly 200,000 BTC or more, had never moved. We found no source for that figure.
fixed: Satoshi announced Bitcoin v0.1 on the Cryptography Mailing List on January 8, 2009, and sent Hal 10 BTC in block 170 on January 12. In a 2013 forum post, Hal wrote that he mined several blocks in the first days and later moved his coins to an offline wallet for his heirs.

title: Hash
wrong: The entry said addresses are hashes of public keys, which keeps the public key private until you spend.
fixed: Most addresses are hashes of a public key or a script, which keeps the key or script private until you spend. Taproot addresses carry a public key directly instead of a hash of one.

title: Lightning Channel
wrong: The entry opened by saying both parties lock funds into a channel's shared output, and its walkthrough mentioned funding by one side only as a variant.
fixed: Usually the side that opens a channel puts up all of the bitcoin. A newer option, dual funding, lets the other side add funds too.

title: Lightning Channel Splicing
wrong: The entry said splicing reached production in 2024, implemented in Phoenix and Core Lightning through a BOLT extension.
fixed: ACINQ added splicing to eclair in April 2023 and to its mobile wallet that July. Core Lightning shipped an experimental version in August 2023 and LDK completed its support in August 2025. Splicing was merged into the Lightning specification in March 2026.

title: Lightning Network
wrong: The entry's note on BOLT 12 offers said they support recurring payments.
